To begin, we identify the centroid, or the average, of a set of vectors \vvec_1, \vvec_2, \ldots,\vvec_n as
\frac1n\left(\vvec_1+\vvec_2+\ldots+\vvec_n\right).
Find the centroid of the vectors
\vvec_1=\twovec11, \vvec_2=\twovec41, \vvec_3=\twovec44.
and sketch the vectors and the centroid using . You may wish to simply plot the points represented by the tips of the vectors rather than drawing the vectors themselves.
A coordinate grid and set of coordinate axes.
A 1\times1 standard coordinate grid and set of axes. The horizontal and vertical ranges both extend from -1 to 5.
The vectors \vvec_1, \vvec_2, \vvec_3 and their centroid.
Notice that the centroid lies in the center of the points defined by the vectors.
Now we'll illustrate an algorithm that forms clusterings. To begin, consider the following points, represented as vectors,
\vvec_1=\twovec{-2}{1}, \vvec_2=\twovec11, \vvec_3=\twovec12, \vvec_4=\twovec32,
which are shown in .
A scatter plot of four data points.
A 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes that contain four data points corresponding to the vectors \vvec_1=\twovec{-2}1, \vvec_2=\twovec11, \vvec_3=\twovec12, and \vvec_4=\twovec32.
We will group this set of four points into two clusters.
Suppose that we would like to group these points into k=2 clusters. (Later on, we'll see how to choose an appropriate value for k, the number of clusters.) We begin by choosing two points c_1 and c_2 at random and declaring them to be the centers' of the two clusters.
For example, suppose we randomly choose c_1=\vvec_2 and c_2=\vvec_3 as the center of two clusters. The cluster centered on c_1=\vvec_2 will be the set of points that are closer to c_1=\vvec_2 than to c_2=\vvec_3. Determine which of the four data points are in this cluster, which we denote by C_1, and circle them in .
The second cluster will consist of the data points that are closer to c_2=\vvec_3 than c_1=\vvec_2. Determine which of the four points are in this cluster, which we denote by C_2, and circle them in .
We now have a clustering with two clusters, but we will try to improve upon it in the following way. First, find the centroids of the two clusters; that is, redefine c_1 to be the centroid of cluster C_1 and c_2 to be the centroid of C_2. Find those centroids and indicate them in
A scatter plot of four data points.
A 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes that contain four data points corresponding to the vectors \vvec_1=\twovec{-2}1, \vvec_2=\twovec11, \vvec_3=\twovec12, and \vvec_4=\twovec32.
Indicate the new centroids and clusters.
Now update the cluster C_1 to be the set of points closer to c_1 than c_2. Update the cluster C_2 in a similar way and indicate the clusters in .
Let's perform this last step again. That is, update the centroids c_1 and c_2 from the new clusters and then update the clusters C_1 and C_2. Indicate your centroids and clusters in .
A scatter plot of four data points.
A 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes that contain four data points corresponding to the vectors \vvec_1=\twovec{-2}1, \vvec_2=\twovec11, \vvec_3=\twovec12, and \vvec_4=\twovec32.
Indicate the new centroids and clusters.
Notice that this last step produces the same set of clusters so there is no point in repeating it. We declare this to be our final clustering.

li.p: We redefine c_1 = \twovec{-1/2}{0} and c_2 = \twovec22. This leads to new clusters C_1 = \{\vvec_1\} and C_2=\{\vvec_2, \vvec_3, \vvec_4\}.
We have new centroids c_1 = \twovec{-2}1 and c_2 = \twovec{5/3}{5/3}, and the clusters C_1 and C_2 are unchanged.
c_1 = \twovec{-2}1 and c_2 = \twovec{5/3}{5/3}. The clusters C_1 and C_2 are unchanged.
